studies.title: Visuospatial working memory and changes of the point of view in 3D space.
studies.abstract: We used functional magnetic resonance imaging to explore the brain mechanisms of changing point of view (PoV) in a visuospatial memory task in 3D space. Eye movements were monitored and BOLD signal changes were measured while subjects were presented with 3D images of a virtual environment. Subjects were required to encode the position of a lamp in the environment and, after changing the PoV (angular difference varied from 0 degrees to 180 degrees in 45 degrees steps), to decide whether the lamp position had been changed too or not. Performance data and a scan-path analysis based on eye movement support the use of landmarks in the environment for coding lamp position and increasing spatial updating costs with increasing changes of PoV indicating allocentric coding strategies during all conditions (0 degrees - to 180 degrees -condition). Subtraction analysis using SPM revealed that a parieto-temporo-frontal network including left medial temporal areas was activated during this 3D visuospatial task, independent of angular difference. The activity of the left parahippocampal area and the left lingual gyrus (but not the hippocampus) correlated with increasing changes of the PoV between encoding and retrieval, emphasizing their specific role in spatial scene memory and allocentric coding. The results suggest that these areas are involved in a continuous matching process between internal representations of the environment and the external status quo. In addition, hippocampal activation correlated with performance was found indicating successful recall of spatial information. Finally, in a prefrontal area comprising, the so-called "deep" frontal eye field, activation was correlated with the amount of saccadic eye movements confirming its role in oculomotor processes.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: fMRI study (NeuroImage, English) examining visuospatial working memory—a core executive function—so meets I1, I3, I4. Abstract does not explicitly state participants were healthy adults (I2 uncertain). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm participant health/status and extract activation data.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This is an empirical fMRI study using a task that probes visuospatial working memory (an established executive function domain). It reports voxelwise, group-level whole-brain SPM analyses (categorical contrasts of task vs. high-level baseline and parametric within-group regressions), with coordinates and ROI follow-ups. At least one within-group task contrast is presented (experimental spatial conditions vs. table task). Participants are a within-group (healthy adult) sample. Whole-brain results are described and coordinates are provided. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/rest-only, not between-group-only, not non-empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I5–I10 and violates no exclusion criteria.

studies.title: All for one but not one for all: how multiple number representations are recruited in one numerical task.
studies.abstract: Number processing recruits a complex network of multiple numerical representations. Usually the components of this network are examined in a between-task approach with the disadvantage of relying upon different instructions, tasks, and inhomogeneous stimulus sets across different studies. A within-task approach may avoid these disadvantages and access involved numerical representations more specifically. In the present study we employed a within-task approach to investigate numerical representations activated in the number bisection task (NBT) using parametric rapid event-related fMRI. Participants were to judge whether the central number of a triplet was also its arithmetic mean (e.g. 23_26_29) or not (e.g. 23_25_29). Activation in the left inferior parietal cortex was associated with the deployment of arithmetic fact knowledge, while activation of the intraparietal cortex indicated more intense magnitude processing, instrumental aspects of calculation and integration of the base-10 structure of two-digit numbers. These results replicate evidence from the literature. Furthermore, activation in the dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex revealed mechanisms of feature monitoring and inhibition as well as allocation of cognitive resources recruited to solve a specific triplet. We conclude that the network of numerical representations should rather be studied in a within-task approach than in varying between-task approaches.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: fMRI study in an English peer-reviewed journal examining neural activation. The number bisection task includes clear components of executive control (monitoring, inhibition, cognitive set changes, working-memory demands) and the authors specifically report contrasts isolating cognitive-set change (bisection possibility; right VLPFC) and monitoring/inhibition (superior frontal gyrus/angular gyrus). Within-group task contrasts (parametric regressors for bisected and non-bisected triplets) are presented. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets I5 (fMRI task assessing cognitive control), I6 (task involves executive domains: monitoring/inhibition/set-shifting/working memory), I7 (whole-brain voxelwise group analyses), I8 (within-group task contrasts), I9 (within-group healthy adult sample), and I10 (whole-brain results reported in tables/figures). No exclusion criteria are met.

studies.title: Cortical activity time locked to the shift and maintenance of spatial attention.
studies.abstract: Attention increases the gain of visual neurons, which improves visual performance. How attention is controlled, however, remains unknown. Clear correlations between attention and saccade planning indicate that the control of attention is mediated through mechanisms housed in the oculomotor network. Here, we used event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging to compare overt and covert attention shifts. Subjects covertly or overtly shifted attention based on an endogenous cue and maintained attention throughout a long and variable delay. To insure continued attention, subjects counted when the attended target dimmed at near-threshold contrast levels. Overt and covert tasks used identical stimuli and required identical motor responses. Additionally, a staircase procedure that adjusted the target-dimming contrast separately for covert and overt trials equated the difficulty between conditions and across subjects. We found that the same regions along the precentral and intraparietal sulci were active during shifts of covert and overt attention. We also found sustained activation in the hemisphere contralateral to the attended visual field. We conclude that maps of prioritized locations are represented in areas classically associated with oculomotor control. The readout of these spatial maps by posterior visual areas directs spatial attention just as the readout by downstream saccade generators directs saccades.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: fMRI study in English with human subjects, meeting I1, I2, I3. It reports group-level, voxelwise/ surface-based statistical maps with permutation cluster correction and provides peak coordinates (Table 1) and within-group task contrasts (shift vs baseline; maintenance vs catch; overt vs covert). Participants are healthy adults and within-group contrasts are presented. Therefore it satisfies the required inclusion criteria and does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, tables/figures).

studies.title: From will to action: sequential cerebellar contributions to voluntary movement.
studies.abstract: The cerebellum is known to be involved in numerous motor related functions, but recent observations suggest that it also performs fundamental operations on nonmotor functions such as perception and cognition. Assuming that the cerebellum has to be consulted in a limited window of time, cerebellar activation should occur in a time-dependent manner in respect to the corresponding telencephalic areas. This hypothesis was tested by combining a simple motor task with the demand of a self-paced delay using event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging. Evaluation with a time-shifted canonical hemodynamic response function revealed spatially and temporally separated cerebral and cerebellar activation accompanying the entire process--from conscious planning to final motor output--within a time frame of 6 s. The cerebral activations spread from the anterior cingulate cortex through the supplementary motor and premotor area to the primary motor and sensory cortices. This cascade was temporally in parallel with cerebellar activations propagating from the neo- to the spinocerebellum. An early lateral cerebellar recruitment 3 s prior movement onset confirms its involvement in cognitive processing. A later medial activation occurring close to movement onset most probably reflects spinocerebellar kinesthetic feedback. Between these two points a striking lateromedial succession was found, which is in line with the hypothesis of the existence of multiple internal models residing in the cerebellum, each communicating with its own corresponding telencephalic region.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract reports an event-related fMRI study in humans addressing planning and cognitive processing around voluntary movement. fMRI and peer-reviewed English-language criteria are clearly met, but it is unclear from the abstract whether participants were explicitly healthy and whether the task qualifies as an executive function/cognitive control task. Insufficient information to confirm I2 and I4, so include for full-text review.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This is an event-related whole-brain fMRI study that tests internally generated, self-paced delayed movements involving intention, planning, and initiation—components of executive function. The paper reports group-level, voxelwise time-shifted statistical maps (15 t-maps) and describes within-group task-related contrasts (task events modeled against baseline), with whole-brain coverage and voxelwise analyses. Participant sample (healthy adults) is acceptable. Results are reported in the text, figures, and glass-brain maps. Full article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

studies.title: Reading minds versus following rules: dissociating theory of mind and executive control in the brain.
studies.abstract: The false belief task commonly used in the study of theory of mind (ToM) requires participants to select among competing responses and inhibit prepotent responses, giving rise to three possibilities: (1) the false belief tasks might require only executive function abilities and there may be no domain-specific component; (2) executive control might be necessary for the emergence of ToM in development but play no role in adult mental state inferences; and (3) executive control and domain-specific ToM abilities might both be implicated. We used fMRI in healthy adults to dissociate these possibilities. We found that non-overlapping brain regions were implicated selectively in response selection and belief attribution, that belief attribution tasks recruit brain regions associated with response selection as much as well-matched control tasks, and that regions associated with ToM (e.g., the right temporo-parietal junction) were implicated only in the belief attribution tasks. These results suggest that both domain-general and domain-specific cognitive resources are involved in adult ToM.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Meets inclusion criteria: English peer-reviewed journal (Social Neuroscience, 2006), healthy adult participants, uses fMRI, and examines executive function/cognitive control (response selection/inhibition) relevant to ToM tasks. No exclusion criteria met; abstract provides sufficient evidence to include for full-text review and possible meta-analysis of executive function activations.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This is an empirical task-based fMRI study that explicitly includes executive-function tasks (response selection/inhibition: Incompatible vs Compatible mapping; and Algorithm construal requiring response selection/inhibition). It reports within-group task contrasts (Incompatible>Compatible; Belief>Photo; task vs baseline) and whole-brain voxelwise analyses including random-effects group-level contrasts (SPM99, reported group results and peak coordinates). Partial-brain coverage (excluding bottom cerebellum) is noted but voxelwise group analyses are provided, satisfying the meta-analysis requirements. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, not non-empirical). Therefore the study provides usable whole-brain executive-function activation contrasts for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

studies.title: Classic identity negative priming involves accessing semantic representations in the left anterior temporal cortex.
studies.abstract: Classic identity negative priming (NP) refers to the finding that when an object is ignored, subsequent naming responses to it are slower than when it has not been previously ignored (Tipper, S.P., 1985. The negative priming effect: inhibitory priming by ignored objects. Q. J. Exp. Psychol. 37A, 571-590). It is unclear whether this phenomenon arises due to the involvement of abstract semantic representations that the ignored object accesses automatically. Contemporary connectionist models propose a key role for the anterior temporal cortex in the representation of abstract semantic knowledge (e.g., McClelland, J.L., Rogers, T.T., 2003. The parallel distributed processing approach to semantic cognition. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 4, 310-322), suggesting that this region should be involved during performance of the classic identity NP task if it involves semantic access. Using high-field (4 T) event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging, we observed increased BOLD responses in the left anterolateral temporal cortex including the temporal pole that was directly related to the magnitude of each individual's NP effect, supporting a semantic locus. Additional signal increases were observed in the supplementary eye fields (SEF) and left inferior parietal lobule (IPL).
studies.abstract_screening_reason: English peer-reviewed NeuroImage fMRI study examining classic identity negative priming—a cognitive control/inhibitory attention task. fMRI methods are explicit but participant health (healthy adults) is not stated in the abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of negative priming, a phenomenon closely related to inhibitory components of executive control. The paper reports within-group voxelwise contrasts (repetition-ignored vs control) analyzed with SPM2 at the group level, including both an a priori ROI analysis (SVC) and an exploratory whole-brain voxelwise analysis with reported peak coordinates. Behavioral and imaging results are presented along with methods, results, and discussion in full. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I5 (fMRI task assessing executive function/inhibition), I6 (inhibition domain), I7 (group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses reported), I8 (within-group task contrast), I9 (participant group reported), and I10 (whole-brain results reported with coordinates). studies.title: Differential responses in human striatum and prefrontal cortex to changes in object and rule relevance.
studies.abstract: Event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to measure blood oxygenation level-dependent responses in 16 young healthy human volunteers during performance of an attentional switching task. The task allowed the separate investigation of lower-order switching between concrete objects and higher-order switching between abstract task rules. Significant signal change in the ventral striatum was demonstrated on trials when subjects switched between objects but not when subjects switched between abstract task rules. In contrast, signal change in the lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) was observed during all switch trials. The switch-related responses were not contaminated by task difficulty, because the greatest signal change was observed during the relatively easy switch trials, which required both lower-order and higher-order switching at the same time. The present data suggest that mechanisms of inhibitory response control in frontostriatal systems are organized according to distinct levels of abstraction. Specifically, the response selection computation carried by the ventral striatum, which projects to the orbitofrontal cortex and the medial PFC, is restricted to the transformation of concrete stimulus exemplar information into motor responses, whereas the adaptive function of the lateral PFC extends to the transformation of abstract task-rule representations into action.

studies.title: Rate dependency of the human cortical network subserving executive functions during generation of random number series--a functional magnetic resonance imaging study.
studies.abstract: In a random number generation (RNG) task subjects are instructed to generate the numbers 1-10 in a random fashion. RNG performance is assumed to involve executive functions, as it requires controlled response generation and suppression of habitual responses. To investigate cerebral structures involved in RNG associated executive functions we investigated functional magnetic resonance imaging in eight healthy subjects while performing an RNG task at two different response rates (1 and 2 Hz). During the 1 Hz condition an activation was detected bilaterally in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (BA 9/46), the lateral premotor cortex (BA 6), the anterior cingulate (BA 32), the inferior and superior parietal cortex (BA 7/40) and the cerebellar hemispheres. In the 2 Hz condition behavioural data showed higher counting tendencies reflecting poorer executive control. In parallel, a homogenous diminution of the activity in the involved cortical areas was obtained. This finding would support the theory of a cortical network involved in executive functions consisting of distinct brain regions working together rather than a distinct fronto-cortical functional localisation.

studies.title: Brain activation during antisaccades in unaffected relatives of schizophrenic patients.
studies.abstract: Schizophrenia patients have difficulty inhibiting automatic saccades. Many studies have failed to resolve whether healthy first-degree relatives share the same deficit. studies.title: Cholinesterase inhibition modulates visual and attentional brain responses in Alzheimer's disease and health.
studies.abstract: Visuo-attentional deficits occur early in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and are considered more responsive to pro-cholinergic therapy than characteristic memory disturbances. We hypothesised that neural responses in AD during visuo-attentional processing would be impaired relative to controls, yet partially susceptible to improvement with the cholinesterase inhibitor physostigmine. We studied 16 mild AD patients and 17 age-matched healthy controls, using fMRI-scanning to enable within-subject placebo-controlled comparisons of effects of physostigmine on stimulus- and attention- related brain activations, plus between-group comparisons for these. Subjects viewed face or building stimuli while performing a shallow judgement (colour of image) or a deep judgement (young/old age of depicted face or building). Behaviourally, AD subjects performed slower than controls in both tasks, while physostigmine benefited the patients for the more demanding age-judgement task. Stimulus-selective (face minus building, and vice versa) BOLD signals in precuneus and posterior parahippocampal cortex were attenuated in patients relative to controls, but increased following physostigmine. By contrast, face-selective responses in fusiform cortex were not impaired in AD and showed decreases following physostigmine for both groups. Task-dependent responses in right parietal and prefrontal cortices were diminished in AD but improved following physostigmine. A similar pattern of group and treatment effects was observed in two extrastriate cortical regions that showed physostigmine-induced enhancement of stimulus-selectivity for the deep versus shallow task. Finally, for the healthy group, physostigmine decreased stimulus and task-dependent effects, partly due to an exaggeration of selectivity during the shallow relative to deep task. The differences in brain activations between groups and treatments were not attributable merely to performance (reaction time) differences. Our results demonstrate that physostigmine can improve both stimulus- and attention-dependent responses in functionally affected extrastriate and frontoparietal regions in AD, while perturbing the normal pattern of responses in many of the same regions in healthy controls.

studies.title: Executive dysfunction in Parkinson's disease is associated with altered pallidal-frontal processing.
studies.abstract: Executive dysfunction in Parkinson's disease is well documented, but it is still unclear whether this results from (i) prefrontal dysfunction, (ii) striatal dysfunction, or (iii) altered striatal outflow to the prefrontal cortex. To clarify this issue, we used H(2)(15)O PET to asses six nondemented and nondepressed patients with Parkinson's disease and six matched controls while they performed a task involving executive function, random number generation (RNG), and a control counting task. To assess the effect of increasing task demands, each task was performed at three rates. Both groups showed significant increase in nonrandomness of responses during RNG at faster rates, which was differentially greater for the patients at the faster rate. The controls showed significant activation of the lateral and medial prefrontal cortex and superior and medial parietal cortex during RNG relative to counting. For the same comparison, the patients did not show any activity in medial frontal structures. The controls showed significantly greater mesial frontotemporal activation during counting than RNG, whereas the patients did not show any modulation of regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) in these areas with task. With faster rates of RNG, the controls showed rCBF increase in the right internal segment of globus pallidus (GPi) and a decrease in frontal cortex. The patients showed the opposite pattern of subcortical and frontal rCBF change with faster rates. The results suggest that executive dysfunction in Parkinson's disease is associated with a failure to modulate frontal activation with increased task demands (nature of task or rate), a deficit associated with altered rCBF in the GPi, the final basal ganglia output pathway to frontal cortex rather than any intrinsic prefrontal dysfunction.

studies.title: Prefrontal mechanisms for executive control over emotional distraction are altered in major depression.
studies.abstract: A dysfunction in the interaction between executive function and mood regulation has been proposed as the pathophysiology of depression. However, few studies have investigated the alteration in brain systems related to executive control over emotional distraction in depression. To address this issue, 19 patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and 20 healthy controls were scanned using functional magnetic resonance imaging. Participants performed an emotional oddball task in which infrequently presented circle targets required detection while sad and neutral pictures were irrelevant novel distractors. Hemodynamic responses were compared for targets, sad distractors, and for targets that followed sad or neutral distractors (Target-after-Sad and Target-after-Neutral). Patients with MDD revealed attenuated activation overall to targets in executive brain regions. Behaviorally, MDD patients were slower in response to Target-after-Sad than Target-after-Neutra stimuli. Patients also revealed a reversed activation pattern from controls in response to this contrast in the left anterior cingulate, insula, right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and bilateral middle frontal gyrus. Those patients who engaged the right IFG more during Target-after-Neutral stimuli responded faster to targets, confirming a role of this region in coping with emotional distraction. The results provide direct evidence of an alteration in the neural systems that interplay cognition with mood in MDD.

studies.title: Disturbances in selective information processing associated with the BDNF Val66Met polymorphism: evidence from cognition, the P300 and fronto-hippocampal systems.
studies.abstract: In this study, we examined whether the Met allele of the BDNF Val66Met polymorphism is associated with selective disruptions to task-relevant information processing. In 475 non-clinical participants for whom BDNF genotype status was determined we used the 'IntegNeuro' computerized battery of neuropsychological tests to assess cognitive performance, an auditory oddball task to elicit the P300 event-related potential (ERP) and, in smaller subsets of these subjects, high resolution structural MRI imaging to quantify fronto-hippocampal grey matter (n=161), and functional magnetic resonance imaging to assess fronto-hippocampal BOLD activation (n=37). Met/Met (MM) homozygotes had higher verbal recall errors, in the absence of differences in attention, executive function, verbal ability or sensori-motor function. Further, MM homozygotes demonstrated a slowed P300 ERP during the oddball task, with corresponding alterations in hippocampal and lateral prefrontal activation, and a localized reduction in hippocampal grey matter. These results are consistent with a subtle impact of the Met allele on fronto-hippocampal systems involved in selective information processing of stimulus context and memory updating within the normal population. The findings also indicate that heritable endophenotypes such as the P300 have value in elucidating genotype-phenotype relationships.

studies.title: Neural correlates of decision making with explicit information about probabilities and incentives in elderly healthy subjects.
studies.abstract: Recent functional neuroimaging and lesion studies demonstrate the involvement of the orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal cortex as a key structure in decision making processes. This region seems to be particularly crucial when contingencies between options and consequences are unknown but have to be learned by the use of feedback following previous decisions (decision making under ambiguity). However, little is known about the neural correlates of decision making under risk conditions in which information about probabilities and potential outcomes is given. In the present study, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) responses in 12 subjects during a decision making task. This task provided explicit information about probabilities and associated potential incentives. The responses were compared to BOLD signals in a control condition without information about incentives. In contrast to previous decision making studies, we completely removed the outcome phase following a decision to exclude the potential influence of feedback previously received on current decisions. The results indicate that the integration of information about probabilities and incentives leads to activations within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the posterior parietal lobe, the anterior cingulate and the right lingual gyrus. We assume that this pattern of activation is due to the involvement of executive functions, conflict detection mechanisms and arithmetic operations during the deliberation phase of decisional processes that are based on explicit information.

studies.title: Opposite effects of catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met on cortical function in healthy subjects and patients with schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) is essential for dopamine metabolism in the brain, and normal variation in the COMT Val158Met polymorphism can influence regional brain function during cognitive tasks. We addressed this by comparing the effects of COMT Val158Met genotype on cortical activation during a task of executive functions in healthy and schizophrenic subjects.

The paper reports group-level, voxelwise random-effects fMRI analyses (load-sensitive contrasts [−1,0,+1]) with whole-brain normalization and cluster-corrected results, and provides coordinates and tables of load-related activations. At least one within-group task contrast is reported for the healthy older adult group. Results are reported as whole-brain voxelwise maps (figures/tables). Therefore all inclusion criteria I5–I10 are satisfied. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, References).

This is a task-based PET study of the Stroop paradigm (inhibition/cognitive control), reporting group-level, voxelwise canonical Z-score eigenimages derived from NPAIRS/CVA (rSPMs) and thresholded statistics. The study presents a within-group task contrast (congruent vs incongruent) and a 12-class model capturing practice effects, with whole-brain PET acquisition and voxelwise preprocessing/normalization. Participants are a within-group sample of healthy adults. Results are reported as voxelwise maps and described in text/figures/tables. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for executive-function task activations and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This is a task-based PET study of dual-task (executive) performance and reports within-group task>rest contrasts in both controls and aMCI patients (meets I5, I6, I8, I9, I10). However, all second-level voxelwise analyses were masked to a pre-defined prefrontal ROI prior to group analysis (the authors state that all contrast images were masked with the ROI mask image yielding 5183 voxels). Therefore the study reports only ROI-masked (small-volume) voxelwise results and does not provide an unmasked whole-brain group-level voxelwise activation map required by I7. This violates exclusion criterion E3 (only ROI / small-volume-corrected analyses with no voxelwise whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I5, I6, I8, I9, I10. Inclusion criterion not met: I7. Exclusion criteria met: E3. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical, task-based whole-brain fMRI study of executive function (cognitive flexibility) using a verbal Trail Making Test (vTMT). It reports group-level, voxelwise within-group contrasts (vTMTB vs vTMTA) with corrected voxelwise statistics and cluster thresholds; results are presented in tables/figures and described in the text. Participants are healthy adults (within-group contrast reported). Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria. Full text includes methods, results, and discussion, so appears complete.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of cross-modal attention shifts that probes executive control processes (cognitive flexibility and inhibition). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (ANOVA and pairwise contrasts) with cluster-correction, and presents within-group task contrasts (Focus-Auditory, Focus-Visual, Shift; task>baseline and Shift>Focus). Results are reported as voxelwise maps, tables, and figures for both older and younger groups. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only contrasts, or non-empirical) are met.

This is an empirical task-based PET study using [11C]raclopride during the Montreal Card Sorting Task (MCST), probing planning/set-shifting (executive functions). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise statistical parametric images of change in binding potential and reports coordinates/figures for significant peaks. A within-group contrast (retrieval with shift vs retrieval without shift) is presented in healthy subjects. Although the multiple-comparison correction assumed a striatal search volume and the authors focused on striatal peaks, the analysis is voxelwise (partial-brain coverage is allowed by inclusion criteria). Results are reported with coordinates and figures; analyses are not ROI-only, connectivity-only, or solely between-group contrasts. Full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical PET study using a task-based paradigm probing spatial working memory (an executive function). The paper reports within-group voxelwise SPM analyses (SWT vs VMT) for both healthy controls and PD patients, including voxelwise statistical maps and reported peak coordinates/tables, satisfying whole-brain voxelwise reporting. It therefore meets all inclusion criteria for executive-function task activations (I5,I6) with whole-brain voxelwise analyses (I7), within-group contrasts (I8), acceptable participant groups including clinical samples (I9), and reporting of voxelwise results in text/tables/figures (I10). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, contains within-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an event-related fMRI task study of somatosensory Go/Nogo paradigms that directly assess executive functions (response execution/inhibition and counting/working memory). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM2 random-effects), thresholding and coordinates, and within-group task contrasts (Movement Go, Count Go, Movement Go vs Count Go, Go vs Nogo contrasts). Participants are a within-group healthy adult sample and results are reported in text and coordinates. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/rest-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). The provided full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

This is a task-based PET study of executive function (planning) using a modified Tower of London paradigm (I5,I6). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise rCBF analyses with statistical parametric maps and peak coordinates (I7,I10). It includes within-group task contrasts (EXPT1 vs 1-move control; EXPT10 vs EXPT1; regression across blocks) for both PD patients and controls (I8), and includes clinical and control participant groups (I9). No exclusion criteria are met: results are not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-state only, and within-group contrasts are reported. Full text (intro, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be included in the meta-analysis of executive function task activations.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study of working memory (an established executive function) that reports within-group and between-group voxelwise group analyses using SPM2 with whole-brain, random-effects contrasts (e.g., VT>FT, FT>FIX). Results are reported in tables and figures, with FDR correction described, and include within-group contrasts for Controls and PTSD. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion, so the full text appears complete. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study of task switching (cognitive flexibility), reporting task-based activation results. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (mixed-effects t-tests, thresholding described) and within-group contrasts (switching vs. nonswitching) are presented for young and older adults. Whole-brain results are described in text and tables/figures. Participant groups are acceptable. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is a PET task-based study of working memory (2-back and memory search), which directly assesses executive function domains (working memory). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses using SPM99 (contrasts such as 2-back vs control and memory search vs control), with thresholding and ROI/SVC comparisons; within-group contrasts are explicitly reported for the sample of older adults. Results include voxelwise activation maps and coordinate tables. The methods, results, and discussion are present in full. Therefore the study satisfies all inclusion criteria for task-based executive-function neuroimaging and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

This study used FDG-PET acquired during mental rest and analyzed pre/post treatment metabolic changes, not a task-based, task-evoked activation paradigm. Exclusion criterion E4 applies because it reports resting-state (or task-free metabolic) analyses without a task activation map. It does not meet key inclusion criteria I5 (task-based fMRI/PET), I6 (task falls within executive-function task paradigm), I7 (voxelwise task-evoked group map), or I8 (within-group task contrast). It does meet I9 (participant group acceptable) and I10 (reports whole-brain coordinates). Full text appears complete. Therefore the paper must be excluded from a meta-analysis of task-evoked executive-function activations.

This is an empirical, task-based PET study of intrinsic alertness (vigilance), which falls within the executive domains listed (I6). The study reports group-level voxelwise analyses using SPM (subtraction of alertness vs control/fixation) and provides coordinates/tables and figures of whole-brain results (Table 1, path analysis based on voxelwise activations), satisfying within-group contrasts (alertness vs fixation). Although the paper emphasizes subsequent connectivity (CSEM), activation maps and voxelwise group contrasts are reported and used to define network nodes, so it does not meet exclusion E4. Partial slice coverage is acceptable per I7 and the study performed voxelwise group analyses. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical PET study using a task-based paradigm that directly assesses visual working memory, an established executive function domain. Group-level voxelwise analyses were performed in SPM99 with multiple within-group contrasts reported (e.g., SPA–AM, NSPA–AM, SPA–NSPA) and stereotaxic coordinates and statistical thresholds provided (whole-brain voxelwise results and figures/tables). Participant sample and methods are described in full (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore all inclusion criteria for task activations (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10) are met, and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

This article is a quantitative meta-analysis of previously published fMRI studies rather than an original empirical fMRI/PET study reporting new human neuroimaging data. It is therefore a non-empirical secondary analysis and is excluded under E6. The paper does, however, analyze tasks that fall within executive function domains (task switching, Stroop) and reports coordinates/tables of whole-brain results drawn from primary studies (satisfying I6 and I10). It does not itself present original fMRI/PET data or group-level voxelwise task activation maps (I5, I7, I8 are not met). Full text is complete and sufficient for screening.

This PET study reports task-based, within-group voxelwise analyses (random-effects SPM) contrasting Emotion vs Neutral conditions (within-group task contrast), and also reports whole-brain results in tables/figures. Although the primary aim was emotion/HRV, the paradigm included explicit task maintenance and cognitive-control demands (working-memory-like maintenance and inhibition) and the authors report and interpret activations in dorsolateral PFC, parietal cortex, and ACC in relation to working memory and task maintenance. Imaging modality is PET and analyses are whole-brain voxelwise, satisfying criteria for executive/cognitive-control task activation mapping. Full article content (intro, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, and I10, and violates no exclusion criteria.

This PET study used FDG during a Continuous Performance attention task (vigilance) in first-episode schizophrenia and reports region-level metabolic results (prefrontal lobe and hippocampus) and correlations. Inclusion: I5 (task-based PET), I6 (vigilance/attention falls within executive domains), I9 (clinical participant group reported). Exclusion: analyses are ROI-based using Talairach-defined ROIs and report region-level ANCOVAs and correlations without presenting any group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps, coordinates, or whole-brain activation maps. Therefore E3 (ROI-only/no voxelwise results) applies. Additionally, the paper does not present a within-group voxelwise task contrast map (main effect of task vs baseline) suitable for inclusion, so E5 (only between-group contrasts / no within-group task activation map) also applies. Full text appears complete (includes intro, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical PET study using a task-based spatial working memory (spatial span) paradigm, which falls within executive function domains (working memory). The PET experiment reports whole-brain, voxelwise SPM99 analyses and voxelwise contrasts (structured vs control; non-structured vs control) with peak coordinates and corrected thresholds, satisfying the requirement for group-level voxelwise task-evoked maps and within-group contrasts. Participants include healthy volunteers (PET) and patient groups (behavioural), so any participant group criterion is met. Whole-brain results are reported with coordinates and ROI analyses in the text. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, and empirical neuroimaging data are reported). The full text provided contains introduction, methods, results and discussion, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This paper reports task-based fMRI of a letter-fluency (executive function) task in ASD and control groups, includes within-group task contrasts (fluency vs control) and voxelwise statistical analyses (voxel-by-voxel correlations and cluster inference using AFNI). Whole-brain acquisition was used and results include voxelwise activation within the left frontal ROI (individual- and group-level activation summary measures were reported). The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria are violated (not solely ROI-summary-only, not connectivity-only, not non-empirical, and within-group contrasts are present).

This is a task-based PET study with whole-brain, voxelwise SPM analyses and within-group contrasts (control vs navigation). However, the experimental paradigm is a visual spatial navigation task and the paper’s focus is on perception, spatial orientation, and cross-modal (auditory) deactivation rather than on established executive function domains (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning, vigilance, initiation). Therefore it does not meet I5 (must assess executive function/cognitive control) and I6 (task falls within established executive function domains). It does meet I7, I8, I9, and I10 (whole-brain voxelwise analysis, within-group contrasts, clinical and control groups included, and results reported in figures/text). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are triggered. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical, task-based PET study of inhibitory control/movement selection (executive function domain). It reports group-level, voxelwise SPM analyses including whole-brain cluster-corrected results and within-group contrasts (isolated index flexion vs full-hand flexion; rest vs movement). The sample (10 healthy adults) provides within-group contrasts. Results are reported in the text with coordinates/clusters and methods (SPM99) for whole-brain and basal ganglia ROI analyses. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10 and should be included.

This PET study administered an auditory continuous performance task (a vigilance task) in a group of 66 healthy adults, so it meets I5 (PET, task-based) and I6 (task within executive domain: vigilance). However, the full text reports interregional covariance/connectivity analyses (Metabolic Associativity Matrix and voxel-wise correlation maps of regional metabolism across subjects) rather than any within-group task activation contrast (e.g., task > baseline) or task-evoked voxelwise statistical activation maps. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (connectivity-only analyses without a task activation map). Inclusion criteria I7 (whole-brain, task-evoked voxelwise map) and I8 (within-group task contrast) are not satisfied, so the study cannot be included for a meta-analysis of task activations.

This is a PET study with behavioural executive-function tasks (working memory, planning), but it does not report any group-level, voxelwise task-evoked activation maps or within-group task activation contrasts. PET was used to measure [11C]raclopride binding (ROI-derived binding potentials) and correlated with behavioural change, rather than to produce whole-brain task activation maps. Therefore it fails the requirements for whole-brain, voxelwise within-group task activation (I7, I8, I9). It also reports only ROI-based PET binding analyses (no voxelwise task activation), meeting exclusion criterion E3. Inclusion criteria met: I5 (PET study assessing executive/cognitive tasks) and I6 (tasks within executive domains: working memory and planning). Inclusion criteria not met: I7 (no group-level voxelwise task activation map), I8 (no within-group task activation contrast reported as imaging), I9 (condition on reporting a within-group task activation contrast not satisfied). Full text appears complete.

This study is a PET receptor-binding study correlated with offline neuropsychological tests (including WCST and verbal fluency) but does not perform a task-based fMRI/PET activation paradigm or report any group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (behavioral tasks used fall within established executive-function domains) and I9 (a within-group participant sample is reported). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (no task-based fMRI/PET activation paradigm assessing executive function), I7 (no group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map), I8 (no within-group task contrast reported during imaging), I10 (no qualifying whole-brain task-activation results provided). No exclusion criteria from the review explicitly apply (exclusion_criteria_applied = []). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study is excluded because it does not provide task-evoked whole-brain activation contrasts required for the meta-analysis.

This is a PET study measuring striatal D2 receptor availability at rest and correlating those measures with behavioral executive tasks. It does not report any task-evoked imaging activation maps or group-level voxelwise task contrasts. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (the behavioral tasks are established executive domains: working memory and planning). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (study is not a task-based fMRI/PET activation study — PET was used at rest for receptor binding, not to measure task-evoked responses), I7 (no whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical map reported), I8 (no within-group task activation contrast reported), I9 (no within-group neuroimaging task contrast reported, so condition for this criterion is unmet), I10 (no qualifying whole-brain task activation results described). Exclusion criteria met: E3 (study reports only ROI PET binding analyses and behavioral correlations with no voxelwise task activation results). Full text appears complete (fulltext_incomplete=false). Consequently the study must be excluded from a meta-analysis pooling task activation maps.

This is an empirical H2[15O]-PET study using a task-based delayed non-match-to-sample working memory paradigm (executive function domain: working memory). The paper reports voxelwise, whole-brain group analyses (task vs baseline contrasts for easy and difficult loads) using SPM99 with tables/figures of activation and group-by-task interactions. Within-group task contrasts (task > baseline) are explicitly reported across subjects and in tables; results are presented as coordinates/activation tables and figures. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so the full text is complete.

The study used PET receptor binding measures and correlated them with WCST performance, but did not report any task-evoked, within-group voxelwise activation maps (no task vs baseline or task contrast imaging). Inclusion criterion I6 is satisfied (WCST is an established executive function task). Inclusion criteria I5, I7 and I8 are not met: I5 (requires an fMRI or PET study assessing executive function using a task-based imaging paradigm) is not satisfied because PET here measured receptor binding at rest rather than task-evoked activation; I7 (requires a group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map / whole-brain evidence) is not met; I8 (requires at least one within-group task contrast) is not met. No exclusion criteria from the list explicitly apply (e.g., the paper does include voxelwise receptor mapping and SVC, but that is not a task-evoked voxelwise activation). Full text appears complete.

This study used FDG-PET during a rest/passive condition and administered the CPT outside the scanner; no task-evoked PET or fMRI activation maps or within-group task contrasts are reported. Analyses extracted metabolic rates from anatomically defined ROIs (subgenual and dorsolateral PFC) and related them to CPT performance, rather than reporting voxelwise, group-level task activation maps. Therefore it fails key inclusion criteria requiring a task-based neuroimaging paradigm and voxelwise within-group task contrasts. Exclusion criteria met: E3 (ROI-only analyses with no voxelwise task activation results) and E4 (resting-state/task-free imaging without a task activation map). Inclusion criteria met: I6 (task used — CPT — falls within an executive domain: vigilance) and I9 (clinical participant group acceptable). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (no task-based fMRI/PET activation), I7 (no group-level voxelwise task-evoked map), I8 (no within-group task contrast). Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical, task-based PET study using an auditory continuous performance test (CPT) — a vigilance/attention task that falls within established executive function domains (I6). The study reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise SPM analyses (Task vs Rest and Rest vs Task) derived from 15O-water PET with thresholds and coordinate tables (fulfills I7 and I10). Within-group task contrasts are explicitly reported (Active minus Rest), satisfying I8. The modality is PET (I5). Participant sample is a human group (healthy adults), satisfying I9. The full text includes background, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext complete). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-group contrasts, and is empirical). Therefore the study should be INCLUDED for the meta-analysis of executive function task activations.

This is a PET receptor-occupancy study that includes behavioral testing of executive functions (working memory, learning) in healthy volunteers, but it does not report any task-evoked whole-brain, voxelwise neuroimaging activation maps or group-level task activation contrasts. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (tasks fall within executive function domains: working memory, learning) and I9 (healthy volunteer group reported). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (the PET data are receptor-occupancy measures, not task-based fMRI/PET activation mapping), I7 (no whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical map reported), and I8 (no within-group task activation contrast in the neuroimaging domain). Exclusion criteria met: E3 (study reports ROI-based PET binding/occupancy analyses with no voxelwise task-activation results). Full text appears complete. Therefore the study should be excluded from the meta-analysis of task activation maps.

This study does not provide task-evoked, voxelwise neuroimaging activation maps required for the meta-analysis. Although it assesses an executive-function domain (vigilance via the continuous performance test) and includes an appropriate participant group, the PET data are molecular FDOPA kinetics measured at rest and analyzed in predefined ROIs; no within‑group, voxelwise task activation contrasts are reported. Therefore it fails criteria requiring task-based whole-brain activation maps and within-group task contrasts.

This PET study uses a task-based auditory oddball paradigm that probes sustained attention/vigilance (an executive domain). It reports voxelwise, group-level SPM analyses (B-A contrasts) for each group using SPM99, satisfying whole-brain voxelwise evidence and within-group task contrasts. Participants include a clinical schizophrenia group, which is allowed. Results are described in the text (SPMs, peak locations, cluster sizes). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so completeness is sufficient.

This is a PET study using an auditory continuous performance task (vigilance), so it meets I5 (PET task-based study), I6 (task falls within executive domain: vigilance), and I9 (clinical participant groups). However, the analyses report voxelwise correlational/functional connectivity maps (ROI-to-whole-brain metabolic associativity) rather than any within-group task-evoked activation contrast (no task vs baseline or task condition activation maps reported). Therefore it does not satisfy I7 (a group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map) nor I8 (a within-group task activation contrast). Because the paper reports only connectivity-style voxelwise analyses without also reporting a task activation map, it meets exclusion criterion E4. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This is an empirical PET study of a working-memory task (face matching) with task-based, within-group contrasts (task vs rest) reported separately for young and older groups. Analyses were voxelwise whole-brain SPM contrasts with reported thresholding and coordinates, results presented in tables/figures, and detailed methods/results/discussion present in the provided full text. The study directly assesses an executive function domain (working memory) and provides group-level voxelwise task-evoked maps (within-group contrasts). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-group activation contrasts). Full text appears complete with methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

Full text is incomplete (API error). Based on the available title/metadata, the study examines PET FDOPA influx related to prefrontal processing of affective (emotional) stimuli rather than an executive function task. Therefore it does not meet the requirement to assess executive function/cognitive control (I5, I6). Because the full text is unavailable, I cannot confirm whether whole-brain voxelwise analyses (I7), a within-group task contrast (I8), or reporting format (I10) are present. No exclusion criteria are clearly met from the available information. Recommendation: exclude due to not meeting I5 and I6; full text incomplete prevents verification of other inclusion criteria.

Although this PET study used task-based paradigms (FDG with an auditory continuous performance task — vigilance) and includes clinical groups (meeting I5, I6, I9), it does not report any group-level, voxelwise within-group task-activation statistical maps. Analyses are based on absolute regional values sampled from 34 predefined ROIs and correlation comparisons across groups (ROI-based/regional coupling). Therefore it fails inclusion criteria I7 (whole-brain voxelwise group maps) and I8 (within-group task contrast). This also violates exclusion criteria E3 (ROI-only analyses with no voxelwise results) and E5 (no within-group task activation contrast reported). Full text appears complete. Excluded for not providing the required voxelwise within-group activation maps needed for the meta-analysis of task activations.

This is an empirical PET study with task-based paradigms (word/pseudoword repetition; encoding/listening to semantic and phonological word pairs) that probe verbal working memory. Working memory is an established executive function domain, so I5 and I6 are met. The analyses include whole-brain, group-level, voxelwise random-effects SPM analyses with FWE correction and reported cluster local maxima/coordinates (voxelwise maps and coordinates reported), satisfying I7 and I10. Within-group contrasts (task vs rest, listening/encoding vs rest) are reported for participant groups, satisfying I8 and I9. No exclusion criteria are met: the study is not ROI-only, not connectivity- or resting-state-only, and reports within-group task activation contrasts rather than only between-group contrasts. The full text provided includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so fulltext_incomplete=false. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria for the meta-analysis of executive-function task activations.

This is an empirical H2 15 O PET study using a task-based Stroop paradigm (inhibition/cognitive control), satisfying executive-function domain requirements. The paper reports within-group voxelwise whole-brain analyses (NPAIRS/CV canonical eigenimages with voxelwise thresholds P<0.001 and cluster extent) and explicitly describes within-group task contrasts (congruent vs incongruent Stroop conditions) with behavioral correlations. Participant groups (first-episode antipsychotic-naïve patients and controls) are appropriate and at least one group reports within-group task activation maps. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met (I5–I10). No exclusion criteria apply: the study does not report only ROI or connectivity/resting analyses, and it includes within-group activation contrasts (so E3–E5 do not apply) and is empirical (not E6). The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete for screening purposes.

This is an empirical PET task-based study that directly assesses executive-type processes (territorial planning and checkmate judgment) using within-subject, within-group task contrasts. The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise SPM analyses (thresholds, group comparisons, and correlation analyses) rather than ROI-only results. Tasks map to established executive domains (planning/strategic decision-making). Group-level, voxelwise task-evoked maps are described for professionals and amateurs, satisfying the meta-analysis requirements. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, only between-group contrasts, or non-empirical paper) are met. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion and appears complete.

This is an empirical, task-based PET study using 15O-water with a continuous performance test (CPT; vigilance) — which falls under executive domains (vigilance) — performed in a within-group design. The paper reports group-level, voxelwise SPM analyses (Task vs Rest and Rest vs Task) across 12 subjects with whole-brain PET maps and coordinates, and presents voxelwise contrasts and tables/figures of activations/deactivations. Electrophysiological data complement the PET but do not replace the voxelwise PET results. All required inclusion criteria are satisfied (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10). No exclusion criteria apply (no ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical study). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This PET study measured striatal DAT binding at rest and related it to behavioral cognitive test performance. It did not acquire or report task-evoked, within-group functional activation maps (no task-based PET/fMRI activation contrasts, no voxelwise group-level activation maps or coordinate tables for task activations). Inclusion criteria met: I6 (the behavioral tasks fall within executive-function domains: working memory and verbal fluency) and I9 (healthy adult participant group is acceptable). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study measuring task-evoked activation; PET was molecular imaging of DAT), I7 (no whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps reported), I8 (no within-group task activation contrast reported), I10 (no whole-brain task activation results reported in any form). Exclusion criteria met: E3 (study reports only region-of-interest molecular binding analyses with no voxelwise task activation results). Therefore the study does not provide the task activation maps required by the meta-analysis and must be excluded.

This is an empirical PET study of executive function (dual-task and integration) using task-based paradigms. It reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM99) including both fixed- and random-effects contrasts (e.g., dual − [auditory + visual], integration − [auditory + visual]) with stereotactic coordinates reported. Within-group task contrasts are presented, results are voxelwise and whole-brain (with small-volume corrections only for a priori regions where specified), and healthy participant data are used. Results are reported as coordinates and statistical maps. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, and not non-empirical). Full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided.

This study used PET to measure brain responses to food taste and satiety (fast vs taste vs satiety), reporting whole-brain voxelwise group-level maps and within-group contrasts (T vs F, S vs F). However, it does not employ an explicit executive-function or cognitive-control task (e.g., working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning, vigilance, initiation). The paradigm assesses neural responses to meal consumption and correlates these with dietary restraint, but the task conditions are not within established executive-function domains required by the meta-analysis. Therefore it fails key inclusion criteria I5 and I6, despite meeting I7, I8, I9 and I10. Full text appears complete.

Although this is an empirical PET task study with group-level voxelwise analyses and a within-group control vs test contrast, it examines implicit motor sequence learning (serial reaction time task), not an established executive function domain (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning, vigilance, initiation). Inclusion criteria met: I5 (PET task-based study), I7 (voxelwise whole-brain analyses / group-level t-maps), I8 (within-group task contrast: control vs test), I9 (within-group contrast reported in a healthy volunteer group), I10 (whole-brain results described and voxelwise t-maps). Inclusion criterion not met: I6 (task does not fall within specified executive function domains). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore excluded because it does not meet the required task-domain criterion for this executive-function-focused meta-analysis.

No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion.

The abstract describes an event-related fMRI GO/NO-GO task probing response inhibition (an executive function). It reports group-level task-evoked brain activations associated with NO-GO and GO responses across distributed cortical and subcortical regions, implying voxelwise whole-brain analyses and within-group contrasts (NO-GO/GO and task vs baseline). Participants are healthy adults (within-group results reported). However, only the abstract/metadata are provided here (no full methods/results sections), so I set fulltext_incomplete=true and assign moderate confidence. Full text review is recommended to confirm that voxelwise, group-level statistical maps (rather than ROI-only analyses) are reported and to extract coordinates or images if needed.

This paper reports PET/fMRI studies of language tasks (hemodynamic responses in language paradigms) rather than executive function/cognitive control tasks. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria I5 (fMRI/PET study assessing executive function or cognitive control) and I6 (tasks within established executive-function domains such as working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning, vigilance, initiation). The provided content appears to be only title/abstract/metadata (no full methods/results/discussion in full), so fulltext_incomplete=true. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are triggered based on available information. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I5, I6 (I7–I10 cannot be confirmed because full text is incomplete).

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of inhibitory control using a stop‑signal paradigm (executive function: inhibition). It reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM99) with within-group contrasts (SST vs NST; UST vs NST), provides Talairach coordinates and figures, and includes methods, results, and discussion. Participant group (healthy adults) is acceptable. All required inclusion criteria are met (I5–I10). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using an n-back working memory paradigm (an established executive function). The paper reports voxelwise, group-level SPM99 analyses (random-effects), whole-brain EPI coverage, and reports significant activations with MNI coordinates and renderings. Within-group contrasts (linear memory-load contrasts and main effects of memory load; memory load × stimulus interaction) are presented for the participant group. All inclusion criteria are satisfied (I5–I10). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not between-group-only, and it is empirical). Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of inhibitory control (Go/No-go), a classic executive function domain. The methods report voxelwise, group-level whole-brain analyses (%AUC maps converted to stereotaxic space, cluster-thresholding) for each participant group and combined maps, indicating whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps. Within-group task contrasts are reported (group %AUC maps for inhibitory trials, and within-subject Time1 vs Time2 contrasts), and results are described in the text and tables. Although slice coverage is partial (19 sagittal slices), the authors performed voxelwise analyses and cluster-based inference, which meets the meta-analysis’ allowance for partial-brain acquisitions. The full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-groups-only, and not non-empirical). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I5–I10 and should be included in the meta-analysis.

This is an event-related fMRI empirical study that directly investigates task switching (cognitive flexibility), an executive function domain, using a task-based paradigm. The paper reports group-level, voxelwise analyses (voxelwise t-tests averaged across 16 participants, thresholded and assessed with Friston–Worsley correction), and presents within-group task contrasts (task switch vs task repetition). Although slice coverage was limited (seven slices), the analyses are voxelwise rather than ROI-restricted. Results are reported in figures and tables. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, and thus appears complete for screening purposes. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The abstract describes an empirical task-based fMRI study of selective letter generation (an executive function/working memory task) that reports within-subject contrasts (selective generation vs an alphabetical control) and describes significant, extensive foci of activation in multiple cerebral regions, consistent with voxelwise, group-level whole-brain analyses. This satisfies criteria I5 (fMRI task-based), I6 (executive function domain: working memory/initiation), I7 (whole-brain voxelwise results implied by reported activation foci), I8 (within-group task contrast), I9 (participant group acceptable), and I10 (results reported in text/figures). However, only the abstract/metadata are provided here and the full article text (methods/results) is not available for verification; fulltext_incomplete=true. Full-text verification is needed to confirm actual voxelwise group-level statistical maps and exact reporting format.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study that explicitly investigates cognitive control/executive-function processes (maintaining intentions in working memory and evaluating actions) using a within-group task contrast (inconsistent vs. consistent actions). The paper reports group-level voxelwise analyses (voxelwise ANOVAs with reported peak coordinates across multiple brain regions) alongside ROI analyses. Although imaging used a limited number of slices (partial-brain coverage), voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and peak coordinates are reported, satisfying partial-brain voxelwise analysis requirements. Participants are healthy adults, and results are reported at the group level. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met (I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, I10). No exclusion criteria apply (e.g., the study is not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical PET activation study using the Tower of London planning task (executive function domain). It reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (SPM) including within-group correlational contrasts of rCBF vs task complexity and categorical task-minus-rest contrasts for each group; results are presented as statistical parametric maps and coordinate tables. Participant groups include both Parkinson’s patients and healthy controls. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met (I5–I10). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Tables — full text appears complete.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study manipulating executive demand (two-back vs one-back; source vs item memory). It reports within-group, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM random-effects) and provides coordinates and conjunction results for sustained and transient load contrasts. Tasks include a canonical executive domain (working memory) and episodic source memory with executive control demands. Group-level contrasts (high vs low load) are reported and thresholded, satisfying the meta-analysis requirements. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical) are met.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using the Stroop task (inhibition), reporting within-group voxelwise contrasts (incongruent > congruent and incongruent > control) with group-level paired t-tests and Talairach coordinates/tables. Methods describe whole-brain preprocessing and statistical analysis; results list activated clusters and coordinates. Participants are native Japanese adults (healthy sample). Thus the study meets all meta-analysis inclusion criteria for task domain (inhibition), imaging modality (fMRI), whole-brain voxelwise analyses, and within-group contrasts; no exclusion criteria are met. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical fMRI study using a go/no-go task that probes response inhibition (an executive function). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise SPM99 analyses and presents whole-brain task contrasts (go vs visual control; go/no-go vs visual control; go/no-go vs go), with tables and SPM figures of significant clusters. A within-group task contrast is reported for the healthy participant group. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (complete). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for task-based fMRI studies of executive function and does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, not non-empirical).

Full text is incomplete: provided content contains only references and metadata (title, authors, DOI). While the title explicitly indicates a PET study of sustained attention (so I5 PET and I6 vigilance/executive domain are inferable) and it refers to humans (I9), the full article’s core content (methods, results) is missing. I cannot verify required inclusion criteria I7 (group-level, voxelwise whole-brain statistical maps) or I8 (within-group task contrasts). No exclusion criteria from E3–E6 are clearly met on the basis of the available content. Because key inclusion criteria cannot be confirmed from the incomplete full text, the study must be excluded pending retrieval of the complete article.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a task-based parametric n-back working memory paradigm (executive function). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM96 group map, Talairach coordinates, tables/figures) and within-group task contrasts across load levels (0B,1B,2B,3B). Participants are healthy controls (within-group contrasts reported). Results are reported as coordinates and figures. The full text includes introduction, methods, results and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met. Therefore the study meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for executive-function task activations.

This is an empirical fMRI study of cognitive flexibility/task switching using a Stroop/reverse-Stroop paradigm. It reports group-level, voxelwise random-effects analyses (voxel- and cluster-level inference), provides whole-brain coverage and tables/figures of coordinates, and includes within-group contrasts (incongruent vs. neutral; parametric modulation of trials since switch). Participants are a human sample (healthy adults). Thus it satisfies I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, and I10. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, not non-empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

Full text provided here is limited to abstract/metadata (fulltext_incomplete=true). Based on the abstract, this is an fMRI task-based study of working memory (spatial n-back) with group-level analyses across 12 healthy volunteers; parametric (load-sensitive) and load-insensitive voxelwise activity is reported in frontal, parietal, and cingulate regions. The study therefore appears to satisfy the review’s requirements: fMRI task of an executive domain (working memory), within-group contrasts/parametric effects, and voxelwise whole-brain reporting implied by statements about preserving spatial resolution and reporting distributed activation. However, because only abstract/metadata are available, I cannot fully confirm the presence of group-level voxelwise statistical maps or the exact reporting format (coordinates/tables). Inclusion is provisionally appropriate but flagged as fulltext_incomplete for downstream verification.

This is an empirical fMRI study of executive function/cognitive control (Go/No-go, oddball, response selection) using task-based paradigms. The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise random-effects ANOVAs and cluster-corrected statistical maps, and presents within-group task contrasts (low- vs high-frequency events, equal-frequency contrasts, errors vs correct). Participants are a within-group sample of healthy adults. Results are reported in figures/tables and fully described in text. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and none of the exclusion criteria apply.

Only title and abstract/metadata are provided (full text incomplete). From abstract, the study is an fMRI n-back working memory task in schizophrenia, so I5 (fMRI task-based), I6 (working memory), I8 (within-group task contrast implied), and I9 (clinical sample) appear satisfied. However, I cannot verify whether the paper reports a group-level, voxelwise whole-brain task-evoked statistical map (I7) or whether whole-brain results are reported as coordinates/figures (I10) because the full article (methods/results/tables/figures) is not available. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are clearly met based on the abstract alone. Because core content is missing and key inclusion criteria (I7 and I10) cannot be confirmed, I exclude the study pending access to the complete full text.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of spatial working memory (n-back), an executive function domain. The paper reports within-group voxelwise task contrasts (Blank minus Simple; One-back minus Simple) and group-level one-sample t-test activation maps, with SPM-based whole-brain normalization and tables/figures of Z-scores/regions. Results are presented for clinical (FASD) and control groups. Although acquisition used 21 contiguous slices (limited coverage), analyses were voxelwise and group-level maps are reported, satisfying whole-brain/voxelwise criterion. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be included.

Only an abstract-style summary is provided (fulltext_incomplete=true). From the available text, the study used task-based fMRI (I5 met).
